newsitem.title: BELGIUM: FOCUS - EU panel fails to deliver EMU budget pact.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - EU panel fails to deliver EMU budget pact.

text.p: The European Union's monetary committee, after 16 hours of talks, failed again on Wednesday to reach an accord on a German-promoted budget stability pact for countries joining a common currency.

Still weary from a marathon weekend session on the Italian lira's re-entry into the Exchange Rate Mechanism, EU sources said the committee was unable to settle differences over several important aspects of the the budget pact.
In particular, the committee remained at odds over how to quantify the exceptional economic circumstances that would allow a government joining monetary union to avoid sanctions.
Under the proposed plan, countries running annual deficits above three percent of gross domestic product (GDP) could face stiff fines if they failed to curb expenditure.
"I think they will present something in Dublin that looks okay," said one source in reference to a summit of EU leaders in Dublin on December 13 and 14. "But it won't be the final version."
Germany, the catalyst behind the so-called stability pact, remained firmly against what it perceives as a watering-down of its initial proposal, the sources said.

Juergen Stark, German state secretary for finance, was said to have continued to back a proposal that includes a two percent annual decline in output as a necessary condition for a country to avoid fines.
The committee discussed a possible compromise, that a decline in GDP of between 0.5 and 2.0 percent would force EU finance ministers to decide whether the economic downturn was indeed exceptional.
There were also differences over the level of fines. EU sources said Germany remained opposed to a maximum ceiling of 0.5 percent of GDP and there was no agreement on the intial level of fines.
The European Commission, the EU's executive, proposed in October a budget pact which included an initial fine of 0.2 percent of GDP with a cap at 0.5 percent.
Another area of contention was where the fines should be deposited. The Commission's idea was to have the initial deposit placed within the EU's budget.
But certain countries argued that such a procedure would benefit all of the EU's 15 nations, including those not participating in monetary union at the start.
Finally, the language of the stability pact was deemed to have less bite than Germany wanted, opening up potential loopholes for governments wanting to avoid penalties.
The work of the committee, comprised of national treasury and central bank officials, now goes to EU finance ministers who meet in Brussels on December 2.
Whether they can resolve the outstanding differences remains unclear, but most expect the outcome to be a "progress report" that emphasises the lines of agreement.

The monetary committee did find a common vision on other issues, such as a new Exchange Rate Mechanism which links the single currency to those who do not immediately join monetary union when it is launched in 1999, the sources said.

It also agreed to bring forward legislation that would clarify the legal framework for monetary union, including the continuity of financial contracts and rules on the rounding of conversion rates when national currencies become "irrevocably" locked to the single currency.
